text.content:
A brute among an outwardly docile clan, Ignazio spent most of his mortal life as a strong right arm for the family's less ethical pursuits. None too intelligent, he was nonetheless effective at his line of work, and the incestuous @UUID[Compendium.vtmlarp.clans.JournalEntry.z724BOvqpVyxjr6o]{Giovanni} branch of the Cappadocians Embraced him as insurance — one of the increasingly rare ghouls elevated into the clan proper as a reward for exceptional service.

Ignazio has acquired some distinction working closely with the @UUID[Compendium.vtmlarp.clans.JournalEntry.phgt6OMwTAoAaKfR]{Lasombra} prince of Venice and with the Doge. Beyond his responsibilities to the Cainite side of the family, he controls several local bands of brigands, lending their use to the prince and the Doge in exchange for favors and other considerations. His tremendous physical power and fearsome reputation have earned him the grudging respect of other vampires, though he remains quite unpopular among the more insular Cappadocian mainstream. With the aid of his gabellotti lieutenants, he helps keep Venice clear of unsanctioned criminal elements and is instrumental in warding off the rampant lupine population outside the city.

Lazarus is a Cappadocian shrouded in mystery. Reports of his mortal life suggest he was a Hebrew thanatologist, Embraced for his vast wisdom and driving interest in death. According to many who knew him, Lazarus was once one of Cappadocius' favorite childer, prized for his erudite thinking and keen insight.

Lazarus sired numerous childer of his own and moved into the lands of Egypt, which most Cappadocians historically avoided due to the insidious presence of the @UUID[Compendium.vtmlarp.clans.JournalEntry.ssX4b2JFXF2uegC3]{Followers of Set}. His stubborn refusal to leave Egypt to the Serpents earned him a reputation for insolence, and he fell into disfavor among the more traditional Cappadocians. Unable to resist the call of a region so heavily steeped in the lore of the dead, Lazarus and his childer established their havens in the shade of the great pyramids.

All contact with Lazarus ceased soon after. Fearing the worst, but not wanting to risk themselves, Caias and Cappadocius left him to his own devices and assumed him dead, in torpor, or under the vile influence of the @UUID[Compendium.vtmlarp.clans.JournalEntry.ssX4b2JFXF2uegC3]{Followers of Set}. But Lazarus was not dead, as Caias discovered when Japheth sent him to check on their estranged brother after the Feast of Folly. Lazarus instead became the most powerful of the Infitiores by default. He has refused all contact with vampires outside his own brood, becoming a secluded hermit in a Coptic monastery, away from the prying eyes of his childer and the minions of Set. Whether he still pursues the eternal riddle is unknown; those who knew him fear the ancient corruption of the land has finally claimed him.

Why Japheth suddenly became interested in his brother's welfare after the Feast of Folly is itself a mystery. The most vicious rumor accuses Japheth of jealousy toward Caias and suggests he hoped Lazarus was indeed corrupted and would destroy Caias; a darker theory implies Japheth is Lazarus, hiding his ambitions behind a mask of feigned torpor while assuming the other identity. Whatever the truth, Lazarus, on the rare occasions he receives company, remains a well-spoken source of lore and legend in the study of the dead.

pages.name: Lord Camden, Chamberlain to the Prince

text.content:
Lord Camden personifies the relationship between the @UUID[Compendium.vtmlarp.clans.JournalEntry.OpCOs3PLjmtl0QVu]{Ventrue} and the Cappadocians. As chamberlain to Mithras, the ancient and powerful prince of London, Camden enjoys luxuries second to none. In exchange for his service to Mithras, he is allowed a wide berth for his experimentation and study — and he is the culprit behind a recent series of nocturnal snatchings, whose victims become the subjects of bizarre tests designed to determine at precisely what moment death occurs.

Camden hypothesizes that death occurs when the soul leaves the body, not when the physical body fails. An ardent follower of the Road of the Bones, he is a radical among the Cappadocians, unwilling merely to accept the work and theories of those who came before him. Believing he must start without any assumptions at all, he argues that the eternal question continues to haunt his clan because its members are blinded by misconceptions of what death actually is — not simply the end of life, but the instant the soul throws off its mortal coil. He points to Cappadocius' own experience with the lone Jew as proof that everything the clan has done to this point may have proceeded from a false premise.

Camden's "grass roots" philosophy endears him to both neonates and many elders: the former enjoy his brash, reflective ideology, and the latter are amused by his vain insistence that they have all been wrong. An accomplished civil engineer besides, Camden usually handles Mithras' less glorious tasks in the administration of the city.

Troglodytia acts as a broker for the Cappadocians and @UUID[Compendium.vtmlarp.clans.JournalEntry.z724BOvqpVyxjr6o]{Giovanni} in her immediate vicinity, procuring dead bodies for experimentation, odd herbs and alchemical ingredients, and any strange artifacts that come to her attention. Though not as unseen as the @UUID[Compendium.vtmlarp.clans.JournalEntry.UhaIbwzsC1O2x9vr]{Nosferatu}, her sympathy with the Lepers gives her access to their vast information network, and she has worked for favors more than once — many local vampires owe her some minor boon or another. She is content to work as she does for the time being, gathering what benefit and promises she can; what will come of the favors she has amassed remains to be seen.

Upon her Embrace, Troglodytia acquired the unfortunate hideousness that has come to afflict many Cappadocians of late. She resembles a corpse in the advanced stages of decomposition, or a particularly deteriorated zombie, and mean-spirited peers gave her the unpleasant moniker she carries to this night. She bears it like a badge of martyrdom, determined to rise above such petty concerns — though she probably never will, as her appearance is so disconcerting that it renders her unapproachable. She cannot meet others in public, nor speak to large groups without offending them with her visage. Though she has taken up company with a group of @UUID[Compendium.vtmlarp.clans.JournalEntry.UhaIbwzsC1O2x9vr]{Nosferatu}, her mastery of Obfuscate is not yet advanced enough to hide her appearance. True to her martyr self, however, Troglodytia has made the best of her lot, becoming a mercenary and a veritable black market all by herself.

Appendix II of the clanbook, "Of Historical Note: What Remains of the Cappadocians," closes the book with a fragmentary, water-damaged letter from a @UUID[Compendium.vtmlarp.clans.JournalEntry.JTrvDnw1eqZyHKuH]{Samedi} elder named Thibault to a childe or correspondent named Emily — the clearest modern-nights confirmation that the @UUID[Compendium.vtmlarp.clans.JournalEntry.JTrvDnw1eqZyHKuH]{Samedi}, the degenerate remnant lineage still practicing Cappadocian necromancy after Clan @UUID[Compendium.vtmlarp.clans.JournalEntry.z724BOvqpVyxjr6o]{Giovanni}'s usurpation, are what is left of Cappadocius' line.

Thibault confesses that he has lied to Emily, if only by omission, in never telling her the whole truth of the clan's fall. He admits the @UUID[Compendium.vtmlarp.clans.JournalEntry.JTrvDnw1eqZyHKuH]{Samedi} are resigned eternally to hideousness, and that the cross of that curse is not an easy one to bear. Their plight, he writes, stems from evils committed centuries ago — evils both of the Cappadocians' own doing and others originating in the Embrace of the "horrid @UUID[Compendium.vtmlarp.clans.JournalEntry.z724BOvqpVyxjr6o]{Giovanni}," whose diablerie of Cappadocius and extermination of the clan's elders left only this withered, hideous remnant to carry on the old work. Once, he notes, the clan could still walk among the Kine, conspicuous but not so grotesque as the Samedi have since become.

Thibault laments that the Samedi still choose their members from those with "a stake in death," but have otherwise lost touch with what composed their legacy in centuries past. No real proof of the clan's true history survives, he admits; barely three or four Samedi remain who lived through the catastrophe of the @UUID[Compendium.vtmlarp.clans.JournalEntry.z724BOvqpVyxjr6o]{Giovanni} coup, and their voices are as silent as the grave they serve. Whatever parallels a scholar might draw between the Cappadocians' historical fall and the Samedi's current wretched state, Thibault writes, are mirrored in the soul of every Samedi cursed to walk the endless night. He closes simply apologizing to Emily for inflicting this truth upon her.
